nameStory: The green sunfish gets its name from its distinctive olive-green coloration that shimmers along its sides and back. Like other sunfishes, it's called a 'sunfish' because of its disc-like, flattened body shape that resembles a miniature sun when viewed from the side.
description: The green sunfish is a small, feisty freshwater fish with a compact, deep body and a notably large mouth for its size. This olive-green colored sunfish typically grows 3-6 inches long, though some can reach up to 12 inches. It's known for being aggressive and scrappy, often punching above its weight class when defending territory or competing for food.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth that extends back to about the middle of the eye - much bigger than other small sunfish. The mouth feels firm and has a slight sandpaper texture on the lips.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Olive-green to brassy-green sides with darker vertical bars that may fade in and out. The body has a slightly iridescent quality that catches light.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, compressed body that feels solid and muscular for its size. The profile is more elongated than a typical bluegill, feeling less disc-like when handled.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Dark spot on the back edge of the gill cover (operculum) and often blue-green streaks on the cheeks. Fins have a slightly rough texture with spiny rays that feel sharp to the touch.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Usually palm-sized at 3-6 inches, though some grow to nearly a foot long. Feels heavier and more solid than similarly-sized bluegills.

habitat: Green sunfish prefer shallow, weedy areas of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They thrive in warm water with plenty of cover like fallen logs, vegetation, or rocky areas. Unlike some sunfish that prefer open water, green sunfish often lurk near the edges where they can ambush prey.

seasonality.spring: Males become more colorful and aggressive as they prepare for spawning, often showing brighter greens and more defined barring. They'll be guarding circular nest depressions in shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to catch, often found in shallow, warm areas hunting for food. Colors are at their most vibrant during the warmest months.
seasonality.fall: Begin moving to deeper water as temperatures drop, though they remain somewhat active. Colors may become more subdued as metabolism slows.
seasonality.winter: Less active and found in deeper water, though they don't become completely dormant like some fish species. Best found near the bottom in the deepest parts of their habitat.

funFact: Green sunfish are so aggressive that they've been known to attack lures and baits that are bigger than they are - anglers sometimes catch green sunfish that can barely fit the hook in their mouth because they were so determined to fight!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with small largemouth bass due to their relatively large mouth and greenish color. Remember: if the mouth extends past the middle of the eye, it's likely a green sunfish, but if it extends well past the back of the eye, it's probably a young bass. Green sunfish also have the typical sunfish body depth, while bass are more streamlined.
compareHints: Green sunfish have a much larger mouth than their sunfish cousins - bigger than bluegills, pumpkinseeds, or redbreast sunfish. While pumpkinseeds have that distinctive orange-red ear flap and bluegills have their dark ear spot, green sunfish are identified more by their oversized mouth and olive-green coloration. They're also typically more aggressive than their relatives, earning them a reputation as the 'bullies' of the sunfish family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's sunfish family, bluegills are distinguished by their prominent blue gill covers and larger mouths compared to pumpkinseeds, lack the long ear flaps of redbreast sunfish, and have a more rounded body shape than the elongated green sunfish.
Among New England's sunfish, pumpkinseeds are the only ones with that signature bright orange-red ear flap.
Compared to its sunfish cousins, the redbreast has the most prominent reddish-orange coloration on its underside and the longest, darkest ear flap without bright borders.
Unlike bluegill and pumpkinseed with their bright colors and small mouths, warmouth are drab and big-mouthed.
